question: Under Rule A.0103, within how many days must a broker notify the Commission in writing of a change in residence address, firm address, or firm name?
choice_a: 10 days
choice_b: 60 days
choice_c: 30 days
choice_d: There is no deadline
explanation: A broker must notify the Commission in writing (which may include online) within 10 days of each change in personal name, firm name, trade name, residence address, firm address, phone number, and email address.

question: When is a business or firm name considered 'assumed' for an individual or partnership licensee?
choice_a: Whenever a firm uses any name at all
choice_b: When it does not include the surname of the licensee(s)
choice_c: Only when the name includes numbers
choice_d: Never - firms cannot use assumed names in North Carolina
explanation: For individuals and partnerships, a name is 'assumed' when it does not include the surname of the licensee(s); an assumed name certificate must be filed and the Commission notified.

question: May a broker advertise or display a 'for sale' sign on a property without the property owner's consent?
choice_a: Yes, if the broker believes the owner would want to sell
choice_b: Yes, as long as the sign is removed within 24 hours
choice_c: No - a broker may not advertise or display a 'for sale' or 'for rent' sign without the written consent of the owner or the owner's authorized agent
choice_d: Yes, if the property is vacant
explanation: A broker may not advertise or display a 'for sale' or 'for rent' sign on a property without the written consent of the owner or the owner's authorized agent.

question: What is a prohibited 'blind ad' under Rule A.0105?
choice_a: An advertisement with no photos of the property
choice_b: An advertisement placed at night
choice_c: Any newspaper advertisement
choice_d: An advertisement indicating an offer to sell, buy, exchange, rent, or lease is being made by the licensee's principal without involvement of a broker being disclosed
explanation: A 'blind ad' is any advertisement by a licensee that indicates an offer is being made by the licensee's principal without the involvement of a broker; all advertising by a licensee must indicate it is the advertisement of a broker or brokerage firm.

question: Under Rule A.0106, within how many days of receipt of an executed contract must an agent deliver a copy to their customer or client?
choice_a: Within three days
choice_b: Within thirty days
choice_c: Immediately, with no grace period ever
choice_d: Within one year
explanation: Rule A.0106 requires agents to deliver to their customer or client copies of any required written agency agreement, contract, offer, lease, or other related transaction document within three days of the broker's receipt of the executed document.

question: Does the 'three-day' delivery provision in Rule A.0106 mean an agent may wait up to three days before presenting an offer to a seller?
choice_a: Yes, agents may always wait the full three days
choice_b: No - an offer must be presented to the seller as soon as possible; the three-day period is an outside limit only for situations where the seller is not immediately available
choice_c: Yes, but only for cash offers
choice_d: No, offers must always be presented within one hour
explanation: The three-day provision does not mean agents may wait up to three days to present an offer -- an agent must present any offer as soon as possible; the three-day period only allows for situations where the seller is not immediately available.

question: If there is already a contract pending on a property and a new offer arrives, must the listing agent still present the new offer to the seller?
choice_a: No, pending offers may be discarded
choice_b: Only if the new offer is higher
choice_c: Yes - the offer must still be immediately presented, though the agent should advise the seller of possible legal risks and recommend contacting an attorney
choice_d: Only with Commission pre-approval
explanation: An offer must be immediately presented to a seller even if there is a contract pending on the property, though the agent must advise the seller that serious legal problems could result from accepting such an offer and recommend consulting an attorney.

question: Under G.S. 93A-6(a)(14), a broker must provide the client with what document at consummation of a sales transaction?
choice_a: A legal opinion on title
choice_b: A copy of the broker's personal tax return
choice_c: A property appraisal performed by the broker
choice_d: A detailed and accurate closing statement showing receipt and disbursement of all monies related to the transaction
explanation: G.S. 93A-6(a)(14) requires a broker to deliver to their client, at the time a sales transaction is consummated, a detailed and accurate closing statement showing receipt and disbursement of all monies relating to the transaction.

question: If a closing statement is prepared by an attorney or settlement agent, may the broker simply rely on it without further action?
choice_a: The broker may rely on it, but must still review the statement for accuracy
choice_b: Yes, entirely -- no further broker involvement is needed
choice_c: No, the broker must independently prepare a separate statement
choice_d: The broker is legally forbidden from reviewing an attorney-prepared statement
explanation: A broker may rely on a closing statement prepared by an attorney or lawful settlement agent, but the broker must still review the statement for accuracy and notify all parties of any errors.

question: How long must a broker generally retain records pertaining to a brokerage transaction under Rule A.0108?
choice_a: One year from listing
choice_b: Three years from the conclusion of the transaction (or disbursement of trust monies), whichever occurs later
choice_c: Ten years from closing
choice_d: Records may be discarded immediately after closing
explanation: Brokers are required to retain records pertaining to their brokerage transactions for three years from the successful or unsuccessful conclusion of the transaction or the disbursement of all trust monies, whichever occurs later.

question: Which of the following must a broker retain as a transaction record under Rule A.0108?
choice_a: Only signed, fully-executed contracts
choice_b: Only advertising materials
choice_c: Offers, even those not accepted, along with sale contracts, leases, agency contracts, earnest money receipts, trust account records, and disclosure documents
choice_d: Only the broker's personal calendar
explanation: Documents that must be retained include sale contracts, leases, offers (even those not accepted), agency contracts, earnest money receipts, trust account records, disclosure documents, closing statements, and other records relating to the transaction.

question: Under Rule A.0109(a), may a broker receive valuable consideration from a vendor or supplier for an expenditure made on behalf of their principal, without the principal's consent?
choice_a: Yes, freely
choice_b: Only if the vendor is a family member
choice_c: Yes, up to $1,000
choice_d: No - this is prohibited without first obtaining the written consent of the principal
explanation: Paragraph (a) prohibits a licensee from receiving any form of valuable consideration from a vendor or supplier in connection with an expenditure made on behalf of the licensee's principal without first obtaining the principal's written consent.

question: Under Rule A.0109(b), if an agent receives a referral fee for recommending a service provider (like a homebuilder) to a party, to whom must this be disclosed?
choice_a: The party for whom the service was recommended, procured, or arranged -- even if that party is not the agent's own principal
choice_b: Only the agent's own principal, never the other party
choice_c: No disclosure is ever required for such referral fees
choice_d: Only the Real Estate Commission, not the party involved
explanation: Paragraph (b) prohibits a licensee from receiving valuable consideration for recommending, procuring, or arranging services for a party without full and timely disclosure to that party -- the party does not have to be the agent's own principal.

question: Which of the following is considered an example of 'nominal' compensation that does NOT require a principal's consent under Rule A.0109?
choice_a: A $5,000 cash bonus
choice_b: A $25 bottle of wine given as a gift to the broker
choice_c: A 1% commission override
choice_d: Free use of a vacation home for a month
explanation: Compensation is 'nominal' if it is of insignificant, token, or merely symbolic worth -- the Commission has cited gifts such as a $25 bottle of wine or a $50 dinner gift certificate as examples of nominal compensation.
source_note: Brokerage Fees and Compensation, Nominal compensation

question: Under Rule A.0109(d), 'timely' disclosure of compensation in a sales transaction may be made orally, but must be:
choice_a: Made public in a newspaper
choice_b: Confirmed only verbally, never in writing
choice_c: Confirmed in writing before the principal makes or accepts an offer to buy or sell
choice_d: Filed with the Commission before any disclosure to the principal
explanation: In a sales transaction, the disclosure may be made orally, but must be confirmed in writing before the principal makes or accepts an offer to buy or sell.
source_note: Brokerage Fees and Compensation, Full and timely disclosure [Rule A.0109(d)]

question: Does the Real Estate Commission arbitrate disputes over the rate or division of real estate commissions between brokers?
choice_a: Yes, this is one of its core functions
choice_b: Only if both parties agree in writing to Commission arbitration
choice_c: Only for disputes exceeding $10,000
choice_d: No - G.S. 93A-3(c) and Rule A.0109(f) provide that the Commission will not act as a board of arbitration for such matters
explanation: G.S. 93A-3(c) provides the Commission shall not regulate commissions, salaries, or fees; Rule A.0109(f) similarly provides the Commission will not act as a board of arbitration regarding commission rates, division of commissions, or similar matters.

question: May a North Carolina broker split a commission or pay a referral fee to a real estate licensee of another state?
choice_a: Yes, so long as the out-of-state licensee does not provide any brokerage services while physically present in North Carolina
choice_b: No, this is always prohibited
choice_c: Yes, without any conditions or restrictions
choice_d: Only if the out-of-state licensee is also licensed as an attorney
explanation: NC brokers may split commissions or pay referral fees to licensees of another state so long as the out-of-state licensee does not provide any brokerage services while physically in North Carolina.

question: What narrow exception under Rule A.0109(h) allows a broker to pay a referral fee to an unlicensed person?
choice_a: Paying referral fees to any friend or family member
choice_b: Paying referral fees to travel agents who contact them to book vacation rentals only, following well-defined procedures
choice_c: Paying referral fees to anyone who refers a buyer
choice_d: There is no such exception
explanation: A narrow, limited exception under Rule A.0109(h) allows licensees to pay referral fees to travel agents who contact them to book vacation rentals only, following well-defined procedures.

question: Under Rule A.0120, may a licensee threaten or force a closing attorney to split their commission with another person or entity?
choice_a: Yes, if the licensee believes it is owed
choice_b: Yes, without limitation
choice_c: No - a licensee may request that the closing attorney disburse payments to third parties, but may not threaten or otherwise force such disbursement
choice_d: Only with a court order
explanation: Rule A.0120(a) bars a licensee from requiring or demanding that an escrow agent or attorney split a broker's commission or pay all or part to another person or entity; a licensee may only request disbursement, not threaten or force it.

question: How many broker-in-charge (BIC) designations may a single broker hold for offices being run at the same time?
choice_a: Only branch offices, never a principal office
choice_b: Up to three offices simultaneously
choice_c: An unlimited number of offices
choice_d: No more than one office at a time, with a narrow exception when two or more firms share the same office space
explanation: No broker may be broker-in-charge of more than one office location at a time, and no office of a firm shall have more than one designated broker-in-charge, with a narrow exception for firms sharing office space.
source_note: Broker-In-Charge, Requirement to Have a BIC [Rule A.0110(a)]

question: Which of the following triggers the requirement for a broker-sole proprietor to designate themselves as a broker-in-charge?
choice_a: Engaging in advertising or promoting services as a broker in any manner
choice_b: Simply holding an active license with no brokerage activity
choice_c: Attending continuing education courses
choice_d: Renewing their license
explanation: A sole proprietorship must designate a broker-in-charge if it: (1) engages in transactions requiring a trust account, (2) engages in advertising or promoting services as a broker in any manner, or (3) has other brokers affiliated.

question: A broker-sole proprietor maintains a trust account solely to hold residential tenant security deposits on property they personally own, per G.S. 42-50. Does this alone trigger the broker-in-charge requirement?
choice_a: Yes, always
choice_b: No - this narrow situation, standing alone, does not subject the broker to the BIC designation requirement
choice_c: Only if the broker owns more than one rental property
choice_d: Yes, but only for commercial rentals
explanation: Maintenance of a trust account by a broker solely for holding residential tenant security deposits received on properties owned by the broker in compliance with G.S. 42-50 shall not, standing alone, subject the broker to the BIC designation requirement.

question: What are the two main qualifying requirements for BIC-Eligible status regarding license status and experience?
choice_a: Five years of any type of work experience
choice_b: Only a provisional license is required
choice_c: License on active (not provisional) status, plus 2 years full-time or 4 years part-time brokerage experience within the previous 5 years
choice_d: A law degree
explanation: To be BIC Eligible, a broker's license must be on active status but NOT provisional status, and the broker must have at least 2 years full-time or 4 years part-time brokerage experience within the previous 5 years (or be an NC attorney meeting alternate criteria).
source_note: Broker-In-Charge, Requirements for BIC-Eligible Status [Rule A.0110(e)]

question: What happens if a broker fails to complete the 12-hour Broker-In-Charge Course within 120 days of designation?
choice_a: Nothing -- the deadline is only a recommendation
choice_b: The broker is fined $500 but retains BIC Eligible status
choice_c: The broker's real estate license is automatically revoked
choice_d: The broker loses BIC Eligible status and must retake the course before being granted BIC Eligible status again
explanation: Failure to complete the 12-hour BIC Course within 120 days of designation results in the broker losing BIC Eligible status; the broker must then take the course again before being granted BIC Eligible status.

question: To maintain BIC Eligible status each license year, a broker must complete which continuing education course, in addition to keeping their license active?
choice_a: The four-hour mandatory Broker-in-Charge Update Course (BICUP), plus one approved 4-hour CE elective
choice_b: A 40-hour annual refresher course
choice_c: No continuing education is required to maintain BIC Eligible status
choice_d: Only the original prelicensing course, repeated annually
explanation: To maintain BIC Eligible status, a broker must renew their license timely and complete each license year the four-hour mandatory Broker-in-Charge Update Course (BICUP) as well as any approved four-hour CE elective.
source_note: Broker-In-Charge, Maintaining BIC Eligible Status [Rule A.0110(g)]

question: By what date must a broker with BIC Eligible status complete the BICUP course and elective CE each year to avoid losing that status?
choice_a: December 31
choice_b: June 10
choice_c: January 1
choice_d: There is no annual deadline
explanation: If a broker with BIC Eligible status fails to take both the BICUP course and one elective CE course by June 10 in any given year when required, the broker will lose BIC Eligible status (and BIC designation, if applicable) the following July 1.

question: A broker who has lost BIC Eligible status wants to regain it. According to Rule A.0110(m), what must they do regarding the 12-hour BIC Course?
choice_a: They never need to retake it if they took it previously
choice_b: They may substitute any four-hour CE elective instead
choice_c: They must complete the 12-hour BIC Course again prior to requesting BIC Eligible status, regardless of when they previously took the course -- there are no exceptions
choice_d: The course requirement is waived after five years of prior BIC experience
explanation: Once back on active status, a broker must first complete the 12-hour BIC Course again prior to requesting BIC Eligible status and re-designation, regardless of when the broker may have previously taken the 12-hour course -- there are no exceptions.
source_note: Broker-In-Charge, Regaining Lost BIC Eligible Status [Rule A.0110(m)]

question: Within how many days must a broker-in-charge notify the Commission in writing upon ceasing to serve as BIC of a particular office?
choice_a: There is no notice requirement
choice_b: 60 days
choice_c: 90 days
choice_d: 10 days
explanation: A BIC must notify the Commission in writing within 10 days upon ceasing to serve as BIC of a particular office.
source_note: Broker-In-Charge, Notice to Commission When BIC Status Ends

question: Under Rule A.0113, licensees must report certain events to the Commission, including criminal convictions, within how many days of the final judgment or order?
choice_a: 60 days
choice_b: 10 days
choice_c: One year
choice_d: There is no reporting requirement for criminal matters
explanation: Licensees are required to report to the Commission any criminal convictions for a felony or misdemeanor, military court-martial conviction, notarial commission sanction, or professional license restriction/suspension/revocation, within sixty days of the final judgment or order.

question: Must a licensee report a Driving While Impaired (DWI) conviction to the Real Estate Commission?
choice_a: No, traffic offenses are never reportable
choice_b: Yes - DWI is a misdemeanor and must be reported under Rule A.0113
choice_c: Only if the licensee was driving a company vehicle
choice_d: Only if it is the licensee's second DWI
explanation: Rule A.0113's note specifically states that Driving While Impaired (DWI) is a misdemeanor and must be reported to the Commission.
